title: Forces change speed, direction and shape
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Physics: forces around us, changing shape, changing speed, changing direction. No textbook needed.
summary: A push or a pull can do more than start and stop things. It can speed things up, slow them down, turn them and change their shape. Your child squashes, stretches, bends and twists things, and sorts them into elastic ones that spring back and plastic ones that stay changed. They measure how far a rubber band stretches, time races to compare speeds, and find that heavy things need bigger forces. Then they test an idea people believed for 2,000 years: do heavy things fall faster?
builds_on: Class 1: a force is a push or a pull. Things don't start or stop by themselves. Every push gets a push back. The Earth pulls things down. Rubbing slows things. Next: Class 3 measures forces in newtons with a forcemeter, separates mass from weight and studies friction. Class 4 explores balance, simple machines, pressure and floating. Class 5 draws full force diagrams, with air and water resistance and rockets.
subconcepts: the four jobs of a force: start or stop, speed up or slow down, turn, change shape
elastic materials spring back. Plastic materials keep the new shape
springs: a bigger pull makes a bigger stretch, up to a limit
a bounce is a squash and a spring back
speed: how far something goes in a certain time
measuring speed by timing a race over the same distance
heavier things need a bigger force to speed up, slow down or turn
the Earth pulls everything down, and without air everything falls together
air pushes back on falling and moving things
pairs of forces: push off and you are pushed back
nature's forces shape the land: wind, water, ice
goals: By the end your child can name the four jobs a force can do and show each one with a ball.
By the end your child can squash, stretch, bend and twist things and sort materials into elastic and plastic.
By the end your child can show with a rubber band that a bigger pull makes a bigger stretch, and say what happens near the limit.
By the end your child can time a race over a fixed distance and say who was faster and how they know.
By the end your child can explain that heavy things are harder to speed up, slow down and turn.
By the end your child can explain why a coin and a sheet of paper fall differently, and why a scrunched paper ball falls with the coin.
words: to press something so it gets flatter or smaller
to pull something so it gets longer
to turn the two ends of something opposite ways
springs back to its own shape when you let go, like rubber
stays in its new shape when you let go, like wet clay
how fast something moves: how far it goes in a certain time
the push of air against something moving through it
a test where you change only one thing so you know what made the difference

days.title: What can a force do?
days.goal: Remember pushes and pulls, then find the four jobs a force can do.

steps.title: Remember last year
steps.do: Ask: 'What is a force?' (A push or a pull.) 'What happens when you push a wall?' (It pushes back.) 'Can a ball start rolling by itself?' (No.) Ask your child to show you three pushes and three pulls in the room in one minute. If they've forgotten, play one quick round of Simon Says with pushes and pulls.

steps.title: One ball, four jobs
steps.do: Use a soft ball and a big sheet of paper. Ask your child to use a force to do four jobs. 1. Make the still ball move (start), then stop it with a hand (stop). 2. Make the rolling ball go faster with a push from behind, and slower with a gentle push from in front (speed up, slow down). 3. Make it turn with a tap from the side (change direction). 4. Squeeze it (change shape). For each job, draw a quick picture with an arrow for the force, and write the job beside it. Pin the sheet up. It is the poster for the week.

steps.title: Force Cards: act it out
steps.do: Print and cut out the Force Cards game (g1). Play the act-it-out round: each player draws an action card, does the action (or mimes it), and says which of the jobs the force did. Ask after a few: 'Can one force do two jobs at once?' (Yes: kicking a rolling ball sideways changes its direction and its speed.) Keep the cards for Day 7.

need: a big sheet of paper and crayons
the printed Force Cards and scissors

days.title: Squash, stretch, bend, twist
days.goal: Change the shape of things with forces, find which spring back, and hear the story.

steps.title: Shape dance
steps.do: Clap a slow beat. On each clap call out a shape and your child's body makes it: squash (curl up small), stretch (reach tall), bend (touch toes), twist (top half turns while feet stay still). Speed up the claps. Then call 'spring back!' and they jump back to standing, or 'stay!' and they freeze in the last shape like clay.

steps.title: Spring back or stay?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child tests each object, says which shape change they used, and puts it in one of two piles: springs back, or stays changed. Say: 'Things that spring back are called elastic. Things that stay changed are called plastic. In science, plastic means it stays in the new shape. It does not mean the material bottles are made of.' Ask: 'Why do you think a sponge springs back but atta dough stays squashed?' Accept any idea. Then say: 'Everything is made of tiny particles. In elastic things, the particles hold on to each other and pull back into place. In dough, they slide past each other and stay where they are pushed.'

steps.title: Story: The Clay That Remembers
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'What is the difference between the clay and the rubber ball?' and 'Why was Paati's handprint still there after sixty years?' (The wet clay was plastic, so it kept the shape. The fire made it hard, so it couldn't change any more.) This story includes a grandmother dying. Give your child time if it brings up feelings.

steps.title: Shape spotting
steps.do: Ask your child to find four things at home that change shape when a force is used: a pillow (squash), a hair band (stretch), a toothbrush's bristles (bend), a wet cloth being wrung out (twist). For each, ask: 'Does it spring back (elastic) or stay changed (plastic)?'

days.title: Springs and bounces
days.goal: Show that a bigger pull makes a bigger stretch, find the limit, and see that a bounce is a squash and spring back.

steps.title: Rubber band stretch
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Hang a paper cup from a thin rubber band, and add coins two at a time. Measure the length of the band each time. Write the numbers in a two-column table: coins, and length in cm. Ask: 'What happened each time we added coins?' (It stretched more.) 'Did it stretch the same extra amount each time?' (Roughly the same. A rubber band is not a perfect spring, so the steps may not be exactly equal.) 'What would happen if we hung something very heavy from it, like a full water bottle?' (It might stay a little stretched, or snap. Every elastic thing has a limit.)

steps.title: Robert Hooke's spring rule
steps.do: Talk about voice v1. Robert Hooke, a scientist in England more than 300 years ago, found the same pattern with springs. He first hid it in a secret code. Ask the voice's question. Then take the spring out of a click pen. Squash it with a finger and feel it push back. Ask: 'Where else are springs hiding?' (A stapler, a clothes peg, a cycle seat, some mattresses and sofas, a pull-back car.)

steps.title: What happens in a bounce?
steps.do: Wet the bottom of a rubber ball or tennis ball lightly. Drop it on a dry tile from knee height, then wipe the floor and the ball, wet it again and drop it from shoulder height. Look at the wet mark it leaves each time. Ask: 'Which drop made the bigger wet circle?' (The higher one.) Say: 'When the ball hits the floor, it squashes flat for a tiny moment. Then it springs back and pushes itself up. A bigger drop makes a bigger squash.' Then drop a ball of dough. Ask: 'Why doesn't the dough bounce?' (It is plastic. It squashes but doesn't spring back.)

steps.title: Start the catapult project
steps.do: Start the project. Tie a plastic spoon to a stack of ice-cream sticks with rubber bands, as in the project steps. Ask: 'Which part bends and springs back to throw the paper ball?' Test it once and keep it for Day 6.

need: a paper cup with a string handle
a rubber ball or tennis ball, and water
a plastic spoon, ice-cream sticks, rubber bands

days.title: How fast? Measuring speed
days.goal: Measure speed by timing the same distance, and feel that heavy things are harder to speed up and slow down.

steps.title: Traffic light walk
steps.do: Play traffic light: green means walk fast, yellow slowly, red stop. Ask: 'What did your feet do to speed up? To stop?' (Push harder back on the floor to go faster. Push forwards on the floor to stop.)

steps.title: Who is faster?
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Mark a 10-step track with two slippers. Time your child walking, hopping, crawling and running it. Count seconds aloud, or use a phone stopwatch. Write the times in a table. Ask: 'Which was the fastest way? How do you know?' (It took the fewest seconds for the same distance.) Then say: 'Speed means how far you go in a certain time. If two people go the same distance, the one who takes less time is faster.'

steps.title: Light cart, heavy cart
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Give the same flick to an empty shoe box and to a shoe box with two books in it, on a smooth floor. Then roll a heavy ball and a light ball slowly past your child, and let them turn each one with a tap. Ask: 'Which was harder to speed up? Which was harder to turn?' (The heavy one, both times.) Say: 'The more matter there is in a thing, the bigger the force you need to change how it moves.'

steps.title: Speed words
steps.do: Say a situation, and your child says 'speed up', 'slow down', 'stop' or 'turn': a cycle going downhill (speed up), a cycle braking (slow down), catching a ball (stop), a bus going round a corner (turn), a bowler's ball hitting the bat (turns, and changes speed). Ask: 'Which one needed a force?' (All of them.)

need: a phone stopwatch or a clock with a second hand
a shoe box and two books
a heavy ball and a light ball of about the same size

days.title: Falling and the push of air
days.goal: Test whether heavy things fall faster, and find the push of air.

steps.title: Which falls first?
steps.do: Ask: 'If I drop a steel spoon and a plastic spoon at the same time, which lands first?' Let them predict and write the guess.

steps.title: The great drop test
steps.do: Do Experiment e5. Drop pairs from your shoulder height onto a cushion, at exactly the same moment: a steel spoon and a plastic spoon, a coin and an eraser, a flat sheet of paper and a coin, and then the same sheet scrunched into a tight ball with the coin. Your child watches and listens for the thuds. Ask: 'Which pairs landed together? When did one land first? What changed when we scrunched the paper?' (The flat paper was slowed by the air pushing up on it.)

steps.title: Aristotle, Galileo and a feather on the Moon
steps.do: Talk about voice v2. Aristotle, a thinker in Greece more than 2,000 years ago, said heavy things fall faster. Most people believed him until Galileo, in Italy, thought it through and tested it. Tell your child that in 1971 an astronaut, David Scott, dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, where there is no air, and they landed together. If you can, watch the short NASA video of it together (search 'Apollo 15 hammer feather'). Ask the voice's question. Then say: 'The Earth pulls everything towards it, and everything pulls back on the Earth. You are pulling the Earth right now. But the Earth is so huge that your pull moves it far too little to notice.'

steps.title: Feel the air push
steps.do: Your child walks quickly across the room holding a big sheet of cardboard flat in front of them, then holding it edge-on. Ask: 'Which was harder? Why?' (The flat card pushes against more air, so more air pushes back.) Then drop a tissue and a leaf from a potted plant, and watch them drift down. Say: 'Air is real, even though you can't see it. It pushes back on anything moving through it. Scientists call this air resistance.'

need: a steel spoon and a plastic spoon
a big piece of cardboard, a tissue and a leaf

days.title: Changing direction
days.goal: Use forces to turn moving things, push off to move, and see nature's forces shape the land.

steps.title: Bounce off a wall
steps.do: Throw a ball against a wall and catch it. Ask: 'Which way did the ball go after it hit the wall? What turned it round?' (The wall pushed back on it.)

steps.title: Marble maze
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Build a marble maze in a shoe-box lid, with straws or card strips as walls. Each time the marble hits a wall, your child says 'direction change!' and points the way the wall pushed it.

steps.title: Where will it go?
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Your child builds the force arrows in the app or shows them with a finger, then answers the 'why' questions out loud before you write them.

steps.title: Rivers and the wind: a small play
steps.do: Show a photo of a river valley or a sand dune, or draw a winding river. Ask: 'What pushed the land into this shape?' (Water pushing on the banks for thousands of years, and wind pushing sand.) Then act it out. Your child is the river and you are the riverbank. The river pushes gently, again and again, and the bank slowly gives way, one step at a time. Swap. Ask: 'Is a river strong or weak?' Then test the catapult from the project once more. Press the spoon down a little, then a lot. Ask: 'Which throws further?' (The bigger bend, because the spoon springs back with a bigger push.)

need: a shoe-box lid, straws or card strips, tape, and a marble or a dried chana

days.title: Show and teach
days.goal: Use everything: the core sheet, the card game, a puzzle sheet and teaching it back.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Read each item aloud. For the arrow items your child chooses the forces and their directions. Talk through any wrong answers using the poster from Day 1.

steps.title: Force Cards: the matching round
steps.do: Play the Force Cards game (g1) with the matching rules: lay the job cards face up and race to match each action card to its job. Explain each match out loud.

steps.title: Puzzles
steps.do: Try two puzzles from Worksheet ws3 together: the one about jumping off a boat and the one about the dough ball. For each, ask: 'How could you test it?' Keep the rest of ws3 for another day.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher, using the poster from Day 1 and the catapult. Ask the check questions as a confused student. Finish with: 'Show me a force changing shape AND direction at the same time.' (A ball squashing as it bounces off a wall.)

Which takes the most force to stop?
Which force of nature made it?
pairs: a mountain valley in the Himalaya

experiments.title: Spring back or stay?
experiments.question: When we change a thing's shape, does it go back?
steps: Pick up one thing.
Choose the right force: squash, stretch, bend or twist.
Let go. Watch carefully.
Say whether it sprang back, stayed changed, or did a bit of both.
Do all the things and make two piles.
experiments.predict: Before each one, ask: 'Will it spring back?'
experiments.observe: Which things go back to their shape and which stay changed.
experiments.why: Elastic materials like rubber and sponge spring back into shape when the force stops. Plastic materials like dough and foil keep their new shape. Paper bends and stays a bit creased. A ruler springs back if you bend it a little, but snaps if you bend it too far. Even elastic things have a limit.
experiments.safety: Don't bend the ruler until it snaps. Pieces can fly.

experiments.title: Rubber band stretch
experiments.question: Does a bigger pull stretch a rubber band more?
need: a paper cup with a string handle (make two holes near the top and tie on a string)
steps: Hang the rubber band from the hook, and the cup from the band.
Measure the length of the band with the ruler.
Add 2 coins. Measure again.
Keep adding 2 coins and measuring, up to 10.
Write the lengths in a table: coins and length.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen to the band as we add coins?'
experiments.observe: The band's length after each 2 coins.
experiments.why: The Earth pulls the coins down. More coins mean a bigger pull, so the band stretches more. With a thin band, each 2 coins add roughly the same stretch, until the band gets near its limit. Spring scales and forcemeters work this way. Your child will use a forcemeter next year.
experiments.safety: Stand to the side in case the band snaps.

experiments.title: Who is faster?
experiments.question: How can we tell, with numbers, who or what is faster?
need: two slippers to mark a track of 10 steps
a phone stopwatch or clock with a second hand
steps: Mark a start and a finish 10 big steps apart.
Your child walks from start to finish while you time them. Write the seconds.
Repeat for hopping, crawling and running.
If you like, time a grown-up walking the same track too.
Put the ways of moving in order from fastest to slowest.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which way of moving will take the least time?'
experiments.observe: The seconds for each way of moving the same distance.
experiments.why: Speed is how far something goes in a certain time. If the distance is the same, the shorter the time, the faster. Keeping the distance the same makes it a fair test. Cricket commentators give a bowler's speed in kilometres per hour.
experiments.safety: Run only on a clear, non-slippery floor or outside.

experiments.title: Light cart, heavy cart
experiments.question: Does a heavier thing need a bigger force to speed it up?
need: a heavy ball (like a cricket ball) and a light ball of about the same size (like a plastic ball)
steps: Put the empty shoe box on the floor and give it one flick with your finger. Mark where it stops.
Put two books in the box. Give it the same flick. Mark where it stops.
Roll the light ball slowly past your child. They tap it to turn it.
Roll the heavy ball at the same speed. They tap it the same way.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Same flick: which box will go further? Same tap: which ball will turn more?'
experiments.observe: How far each box goes and how much each ball turns.
experiments.why: The more mass (matter) something has, the more force it takes to change its speed or direction. That's why a heavy ball hardly turns when tapped, and a light one swerves. Scientists call this inertia.
experiments.safety: Roll the heavy ball slowly and keep feet clear.

experiments.title: The great drop test
experiments.question: Do heavy things fall faster than light things?
need: a steel spoon and a plastic spoon
two sheets of the same paper
steps: Hold two things at exactly the same height, at your shoulder.
Let go at exactly the same moment. Your child watches and listens for the thuds.
Do steel spoon and plastic spoon. Coin and eraser.
Do a flat sheet of paper and the coin.
Scrunch one sheet into a tight ball and drop it with the coin.
Repeat each pair twice.
experiments.predict: Ask before each pair: 'Which will land first?'
experiments.observe: Which lands first, or whether they land together.
experiments.why: Without air, everything falls at the same rate, whatever it weighs. Spoons, coins and erasers are small and compact, so the air hardly slows them, and they land almost together. A flat sheet has a big surface for the air to push up on, so it falls slowly. Scrunching the same paper leaves the air much less to push on, so it falls almost as fast as the coin. The difference comes from the air, not the weight.
experiments.safety: Drop things onto a cushion, away from feet.

activities.title: Marble maze
need: a marble, or a dried chana
steps: Draw a start and a finish on the lid.
Glue straws or card strips as walls to make a twisting path.
Tilt the lid to roll the marble from start to finish.
Each time the marble hits a wall, say 'direction change!'
Make it harder with more turns.
activities.outcome: A working maze, and a child who can explain that each wall pushes the marble a new way.

project.title: Design a catapult
steps: Make a spoon catapult: tie a plastic spoon to a block or a stack of ice-cream sticks with rubber bands.
Load a paper ball and press down the spoon. Let go.
Change one thing at a time: press further down, or use two rubber bands.
Measure how far the ball goes each time in steps.
Explain which part is bending and springing back, and why a bigger bend throws further.
project.outcome: A working catapult and a chart of what made it shoot further.

game.title: Force Cards
rules: Cut out the cards. There are action cards (white) and job cards (coloured).
Act-it-out round: shuffle the action cards. Take one, do the action, and say what the force did. Right: keep the card.
Matching round: lay the 6 job cards face up. Turn over action cards one at a time. The first to slap the right job card and explain wins the action card.
Some actions do two jobs. If you can name both, take a bonus card.

cards.back: change direction (and shape for a moment)

big: When you sit on a chair, are you pushing it? Is it pushing you?
Why do some things spring back after a push, and others stay changed?
Is a river strong or gentle?
If there were no air, how would a feather fall?
Is faster always better? When is slow better?

challenge.q: There's a famous story that Galileo dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Did that really happen?
challenge.hint: The only record is from his student and first biographer, Vincenzo Viviani, written many years later, and Galileo never wrote about it himself. Many historians doubt it. What we do know: he did careful tests with balls rolling down ramps. Ask: why might a story be remembered even if it isn't true?

challenge.q: People say 'heavy things fall faster'. Is that always wrong?
challenge.hint: Drop a sheet of paper and a coin: the coin wins. Now scrunch the paper into a tight ball and try again. What changed? It's the air, not the weight. In everyday life, heavy compact things often do land first, which is why the idea lasted so long.

challenge.q: We say rubber is 'stretchy' and steel is 'stiff'. Is steel elastic?
challenge.hint: Yes! Steel springs back too, it just needs a much bigger force to stretch or bend it. That's why springs and the spokes of a cycle wheel are made of steel. Scientists call a material elastic if it returns to its shape, however hard it is to bend.

perspectives.who: A potter in Manamadurai, Tamil Nadu
perspectives.view: A potter squashes, pulls and bends wet clay to shape a pot. Wet clay is plastic, so it keeps the shape the potter gives it. Ask: why can't you shape a pot once the clay is dry? What does the kiln's heat do to the clay?
A spin bowler twists the ball as it leaves the hand, so it changes direction when it bounces. A fast bowler uses speed. Ask: which forces did the bowler use, and which did the pitch use?
A river pushes on its banks every second of every day. Over thousands of years, that push carves valleys and canyons. Ask: is a river strong or weak? What would a riverbank say about the river?

A spider catches food in a web. A flying insect hits the web hard and fast. The silk stretches and springs back, so the web holds the insect without breaking. Ask: what would happen to a web that could not stretch?

voices.idea: Hooke found that a spring stretches more when you hang more weight on it, and that the stretch grows in step with the weight. He first published it as a Latin anagram in 1676 so nobody could steal it, and explained it in 1678: 'as the extension, so the force'.
voices.then: It was accepted, and became known as Hooke's law. Hooke also worked on springs for watches.
voices.now: Still accepted, with a limit. Stretch a spring or band too far and it stops following the rule. It stays stretched or snaps. Hooke was also the first to use the word 'cell' for the tiny parts of living things. He quarrelled with Isaac Newton over who first thought of how gravity weakens with distance.
voices.ask: Our rubber band followed the pattern for a while. What happened near the end? Why do you think a rule might stop working?

voices.who: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), Greece, and Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italy
voices.idea: Aristotle taught that heavier things fall faster than light ones, in proportion to their weight.
voices.then: Galileo argued against it. He imagined tying a heavy stone to a light stone: would the pair fall faster (it's heavier) or slower (the light one holds it back)? Both can't be true, so the idea must be wrong. He then tested balls on ramps.
voices.now: Galileo was right: without air, everything falls at the same rate. In 1971 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, where there's no air, and they landed together.
voices.ask: Our spoons landed together but the flat paper didn't. Does that mean Galileo was wrong, or is something else going on? How did scrunching the paper help us decide?

books.why: A good refresher on what forces do.

check.q: Name four things a force can do.
check.a: Start or stop something, speed it up or slow it down, change its direction, change its shape.

check.q: Show me squash, stretch, bend and twist. Which things spring back?
check.a: Any correct action for each. Elastic things like rubber and sponge spring back. Plastic things like dough stay changed.

check.q: What happened when we added more coins to the rubber band?
check.a: It stretched more, because the pull was bigger, until it got near its limit.

check.q: Two children walk the same 10 steps. One takes 6 seconds and one takes 9. Who is faster?
check.a: The one who took 6 seconds: less time for the same distance.

check.q: Why is a heavy ball harder to turn than a light one?
check.a: It has more mass, so it needs a bigger force to change how it moves.

check.q: Do heavy things always fall faster?
check.a: No. Without air they fall together. Air slows down light, spread-out things like feathers and flat paper.

check.q: What turns a ball round when it hits a wall?
check.a: The wall pushes back on it.

story.title: The Clay That Remembers
text: In Manamadurai, a town in Tamil Nadu where the potters' wheels hum from morning till night, there lived a girl called Lakshmi and her grandmother, Paati. Paati's hands were brown and cracked, like a dry riverbed in May, and they could do wonderful things. Lakshmi had watched them a thousand times: a lump of wet grey clay on the spinning wheel, Paati's thumbs pressing down into its middle, her fingers pulling up its sides, and a pot rising out of nothing like a flower opening.
"How does the clay know what to become?" Lakshmi asked.

"I don't know what clay knows," said Paati. "But I know this. Every push and every pull my hands give it, the clay keeps. A rubber ball doesn't keep anything. Squeeze it, let go, and it jumps back, as if nothing happened. But clay keeps every touch."

Lakshmi tried it. She pressed her thumb into a soft lump of clay. When she lifted it, her thumbprint was still there, with every tiny swirl. She squeezed a rubber ball in her other hand and let go. Pop, back to round. The ball was round again, as if she had never touched it.

After that she tested everything. The hair band on her plait stretched when she pulled it, and went small again when she let go. The tin lid she sat on by mistake stayed bent. Her own cheek, when Paati pinched it, sprang back at once, which made Paati laugh. "You are made of rubber," she said. "Good. Children should spring back."
"Can I make the clay lose a shape, if I want to?" Lakshmi asked.

"Only while it's wet," said Paati. She squashed the thumbprint flat with the heel of her hand, and it was gone. "Push it gently and it changes a little. Push it hard and it changes a lot. But once it goes into the fire, it keeps its shape for ever. The fire turns soft clay as hard as stone."
That rainy season Paati grew tired, and then she grew ill. She stopped going to the wheel. The house was quiet in a way Lakshmi didn't like. When the paddy fields turned gold, Paati died.

Lakshmi didn't want to go near the wheel after that. For weeks it stood still under its cloth. One day her mother asked her to fetch the big old water pot from the storeroom, the one that had been in the family longer than anyone could say. It was heavy and cool, and as Lakshmi carried it into the light, she saw something on its side, near the bottom, that she had never noticed before.
A handprint. A small one, pressed into the clay before it was baked, a long, long time ago. And next to it, a bigger one.

Her mother knelt beside her and put her finger in the small handprint. "That," she said, "is Paati's hand, when she was about your age. And that big one is her mother's. She was teaching Paati, like Paati taught you."

Lakshmi put her own hand next to the small one. It was almost exactly the same size. The clay had kept Paati's push for sixty years. The fire had made it hard, so the handprint could never be squashed out again.

The next morning Lakshmi took the cloth off the wheel. She wet the clay the way Paati had shown her. She pushed her thumbs into its middle and pulled its walls up, slowly, wobbly, a little lopsided. It wasn't a good pot. But before it went into the kiln, she pressed her hand into its side, and her mother pressed hers next to it.
"Some things spring back," Lakshmi said, looking at the two handprints. "And some things keep the shape you give them."
Her mother didn't answer. She just held Lakshmi's clay-covered hand for a long time.
story.epiphany: Forces change shape. Elastic things (a rubber ball, a hair band, a child's cheek) spring back when the force stops. Plastic things (wet clay, a bent tin lid) keep the new shape. Firing in a kiln makes clay hard, so its shape can't change any more. The story turns on the old handprint on the water pot.
ask: What's the difference between the clay and the rubber ball?
Why was Paati's handprint still there after sixty years?
Find three things at home that spring back after a push, and three that stay changed.
What did Paati mean when she said children should spring back?
The handprint stayed for sixty years. What else around you still shows a push or a press from long ago?

ideas.idea: Forces can change the shape of things, and some things keep the new shape.
ideas.more: Rubber, sponges and springs are elastic: they spring back. Clay, dough and foil are plastic: they stay changed. Over thousands of years, a river's push on its banks can carve a whole valley.

ideas.idea: Changing speed or direction always needs a force, and heavy things need bigger ones.
ideas.more: A ball going round a bend, a bus turning a corner, a loaded truck braking: something is always pushing or pulling them. The more mass a thing has, the harder it is to change how it moves.

ideas.idea: Everything falls at the same rate when there's no air.
ideas.more: A hammer and a feather landed together on the Moon in 1971. Heavy things don't fall faster. Air is what slows the light, spread-out ones.

unknowns: How is spider silk so strong and so stretchy at the same time? For its weight, it is tougher than steel. Scientists are still working out exactly how spiders spin it, and nobody can yet make anything as good.
Why does all matter fall at the same rate? Einstein explained it by saying that falling things follow curves in space and time, but why mass curves space at all, nobody knows.

Why do some materials spring back and others stay put? Scientists understand a lot about atoms sliding or holding on, but they still can't fully predict how a new material will stretch, bend or break without testing it.
